review_basis: Original numbered AIF Module 03 WebP slides 30–32 individually inspected in display order; narration follows actual labels, arrows, examples and decision cues.

scenes.title: Semi-supervised learning
scenes.narration: This slide introduces a middle ground between fully labeled examples and a large collection with no human labels. Look first at the small labeled dataset on the upper left: two cats and two dogs have their correct names attached. Under it is a much larger collection of pet photographs without labels. Labeling every photograph by hand takes time and money. Semi-supervised learning uses the small trusted set together with the larger unlabeled set. Follow the three numbered steps. First, train an initial model on the labeled cat and dog photographs. Second, use it to guess categories for unlabeled images. These guesses are called pseudo-labels, because they come from a model rather than an original trusted annotation. The visual shows cat with confidence zero point nine five and dog with zero point nine two, alongside less confident predictions of zero point six and zero point five five. A confidence score is not a guarantee that a prediction is correct. The orange warning explicitly says pseudo-labels can be wrong, particularly when confidence is low. Third, select carefully reviewed or sufficiently reliable pseudo-labels, add them to the original training data, and retrain. Incorrect labels can reinforce mistakes, so this process requires evaluation and sometimes human checks. The bottom panels repeat the distinction between labeled and unlabeled photographs and show a low-confidence cat guess being rejected or reviewed. A simple example is a school with a few accurately categorized messages and many uncategorized messages. It may use the existing labels to help learn from the remaining messages, but should not blindly trust its own predictions. Check: is semi-supervised learning the same as inventing ground truth for every example? No. The extra labels are provisional and require filtering and quality controls.

scenes.title: Self-Supervised Learning Huge amount of text data
scenes.narration: On this slide, we meet self-supervised learning. It learns from data by creating a prediction task using information already inside that data. Start with the large stack of documents at the left: books, articles, websites and other text, without human-assigned class labels. Follow the arrow to the masked sentence, the cat sat on the mask. The original sentence supplies the word that was hidden. The system does not need a person to write a separate spam, topic or sentiment label for every sentence. By trying to predict hidden or next words across many examples, a model can learn patterns in grammar, vocabulary and relationships between words. The central neural network represents training, while the right panel lists the useful representations and patterns that can later be applied to specific tasks. The lower-left everyday analogy shows a person who has read many sentences and can guess a missing word such as mat because the surrounding context provides clues. Remember that self-supervised learning does not mean the model understands everything correctly or never needs evaluation. The center lower panel notes natural language models such as BERT and GPT, while the other example shows that images can also support self-supervised tasks when their hidden or rearranged pieces become training signals. The bottom right says to consider this approach when you have many unlabeled examples and can define a meaningful prediction task. A crucial distinction from the previous slide: semi-supervised learning mixes some human labels with unlabeled data; self-supervised learning constructs a learning signal from the input itself. What gives the training answer to a masked word? The original unmasked text, not a separate human-created class label.

scenes.title: Self-supervised learning: predicting missing content
scenes.narration: Here the slide makes the self-supervised process more concrete. Begin with the left input card. The sentence reads, the gardener waters the flowers each morning. We have a complete sentence, but it does not have a separate human-written category label. Step two hides the word flowers and presents the sentence to the model as the gardener waters the mask each morning. The original word flowers becomes the target for this temporary task. This is called a pretext task: a training exercise designed to help the model acquire useful patterns even if filling a blank is not the final business task. The arrow leads to the representation network in the center. By repeatedly learning to recover missing information, the model can develop numerical representations of language context and relationships. Notice that the diagram does not claim it must memorize every sentence. The goal is to learn reusable information. Finally, the right panel lists downstream tasks: text classification, summarization and question answering. A downstream task is the real job we want the model to perform after learning general patterns. Depending on the application, it may require further training, fine-tuning, instructions or other system components. The bottom decision cue says to use self-supervised learning when we have abundant unlabeled information and can define a meaningful prediction exercise, such as predicting masked, next or hidden content. Here is a quick decision check. A company has millions of documents but almost no category labels, and wants to pretrain a general language representation. Would self-supervised learning help? Yes, because the documents themselves can provide prediction targets. Does that remove the need to test the system on real tasks? No. Those tasks still need suitable evaluation.
